UNITED STATES OF AMERICA
                                           BEFORE THE
                             FEDERAL ENERGY REGULATORY COMMISSION

PJM Interconnection, L.L.C., et al.                                     )                 Docket No. EL25-49-000
                                                                        )                 Docket No. EL25-49-001

PJM Interconnection, L.L.C.                                             )

                             MOTION FOR LEAVE AND ANSWER OF
                          CONSTELLATION ENERGY GENERATION, LLC

           Constellation moves for leave and submits this answer1 to reject four arguments made by

PJM and the Indicated PJM Transmission Owners in their response briefs.2 First, just and

reasonable rules for large load interconnection cannot be delayed until the end of the decade and

claims that such delays are “required”3 are belied both by PJM’s rush to adopt its own preferred

“Connect and Manage” alternative and by the fact that other regions are managing to develop rules

for interruptibility much more quickly. Second, the Federal Power Act (“FPA”) requires study

requirements to be clearly written in the PJM Tariff because these study timelines and

methodologies significantly affect the provision of the new transmission services—and a lack of

 clarity and resulting protracted delays (including delays due to refusals to study) are what

instigated this proceeding in the first place. Third, draconian rules imposing disqualifications,

suspensions and other unnecessary restrictions on the Commission’s new transmission services do

not address any genuine “risks to reliability and resource adequacy”4 but instead merely limit

access to, frustrate, and otherwise discriminate against these landmark services. Fourth, the

Transmission Owners’ excessive Grid Reliance Charge has no basis in principle or precedent,

while Constellation has proposed a just and reasonable replacement rate the Commission can

readily adopt. In addition, there are several other areas in PJM’s response brief and revised

Illustrative Tariff where clarification is needed or appropriate.

     I.     Three Years Is Not “Required” to Replace an Unlawful Rate

            PJM claims “[a] June 1, 2029 effective date is required for the provision of these new,

curtailable services.”5 At the same time, PJM is expediting its Connect and Manage

interconnection framework to commence June 1, 2027, which would allow the interconnection of

non-capacity backed loads that are potentially interruptible during capacity shortages, unless the

load brings its own (new) generation.6 This, ironically, is a rebranded Option 7 from PJM’s show-

cause filing, which the Commission rejected in favor of Interim Network Integration Transmission

Service (“Interim NITS”).7 PJM did not seek rehearing on this point, yet PJM is nonetheless fast-

tracking the version of interruptibility that the Commission rejected, while slow-boating the

credible that PJM will take more than three years to implement Interim NITS allegedly due to

“significant changes to PJM’s core Markets and Operations systems”8 but less than one year to

commence Connect and Manage, a framework not clearly defined let alone demonstrated to be

just and reasonable.

            Accordingly, the Commission should promptly approve the rates and terms for Interim

NITS, with Constellation’s focused modifications,9 and make them effective no later than

October 1, 2026, so that service can begin no later than June 1, 2027, the same date that PJM plans

to commence Connect and Manage. Adopting Interim NITS as soon as possible—for pending and

future NITS applicants—should not be difficult. PJM “designed the new Interim NITS to basically

be treated the same as regular, full NITS.”10

    II.     Study Procedures and Deadlines Must Be in the Tariff

            The study procedures for the new transmission services must be identified clearly and

spelled out in the tariff. Indeed, additional studies may not be needed at all to implement Interim

NITS. As PJM states, it could determine that “the NITS study already conclusively answers the

question of whether and how much Interim NITS may be provided” and grant Interim NITS

“immediately.”11 PJM nevertheless argues, first, that its Illustrative Tariff properly details how

studies are outside the scope of the Commission’s jurisdiction.13 Neither argument has merit.

                       A. The Commission Should Require Clear and Detailed Study Requirements to
                          be on File

            The Illustrative Tariff does not contain any clear statement of what studies will be required

for the new transmission services. Rather, it states merely that PJM will determine “whether

additional studies are needed”14 for Interim NITS and “will coordinate with the affected

Transmission Owner(s) to complete studies, including load integration studies”15 for Contract

Demand Services. Contrary to PJM’s assertions, these vague statements do not come close to

“appropriately detail[ing] PJM’s process, role, and standards for studying requests for these new

transmission services.”16 Indeed, the only “detail” that can be gleaned from the Illustrative Tariff

is that studies may be conducted. There is no indication of what type of studies will be conducted—

other than the Transmission Owners’ load integration studies—or the methodologies PJM will use

to assess whether the transmission system can “reliably” provide the new transmission services.

            These are not mere “implementation” details that are missing from the Illustrative Tariff.

These terms directly affect eligibility for Interim NITS and Contract Demand Services, which

clearly is a core requirement of the service.17 Requirements establishing the type of studies

performed and methodologies used to assess whether PJM can provide the new transmission

susceptible of specification, and that are not so generally understood in any contractual

arrangement as to render recitation superfluous.”18 PJM has a “statutory obligation to file

significant changes to its rates and ‘practices … affecting such rates.’”19 It is irrelevant whether

stakeholders have the “fulsome opportunity to participate”20 in the development of PJM’s Manuals

because including this material is part of PJM’s compliance obligation.21

            Accordingly, the Commission should direct PJM to set forth clear and specific study

requirements in the Tariff. At a minimum, PJM should specify in its Tariff the violations that will

be studied and the studies to be conducted for each, the deadline for completing each study and

steps taken if study deadlines are not met, and defined remediation for specific violations found.

The record in this long proceeding underscores that it is critical for these study rules and deadlines

to be on file to effectuate the Commission’s and the Trump Administration’s commitment to

providing prompt service to large loads.22

                      B. Transmission Owner Load Integration Study Requirements are Unwritten
                        and Undisclosed Policies that Significantly Affect the Commission’s
                        Landmark Transmission Services

            The Commission has jurisdiction to regulate load integration studies in connection with

jurisdictional transmission service. PJM is wrong to assert that “any ‘lack of detail’” regarding

those studies is justified for jurisdictional reasons.23 The Commission has jurisdiction over all

transmissions, including transmissions to end users.24 The courts have long held the Commission

can regulate practices affecting rates within its jurisdiction, even if the Commission’s regulation

touches upon state authority.25 Load integration studies, which determine “whether (and to what

            On rehearing, and on its own accord,27 the Commission should exercise its jurisdiction over

the load integration studies needed to provide jurisdictional transmission service and direct those

load integration studies to be on file.28 At a minimum, the PJM Tariff should specify the violations

that will be studied and the studies to be conducted for each, the deadline for completing each

study and steps taken if study deadlines are not met, and define remediation for specific violations

found. Otherwise, the Commission risks neutering its December 18th Order by allowing

recalcitrant Transmission Owners an avenue to delay or disfavor the Commission’s new

transmission services.29

III.        The Commission Should Reject Certain Proposed Strictures on the New Transmission

Commission should reject both.

                    A. PJM’s Proposed Disqualification and Suspension Scheme is Not a Just,
                       Reasonable and Non-Discriminatory Replacement Rate

            PJM fails to demonstrate that “unique reliability and resource adequacy risks” justify the

extreme and unprecedented penalties PJM proposes with respect to the Commission’s new

transmission services.

            First, existing practice shows that PJM’s proposal is unwarranted. PJM Transmission

Customers taking Non-Firm Point-To-Point Transmission Service are not subject to suspension or

disqualification for unreserved use of the transmission system.32 PJM provides no reason why

customers taking the new non-firm transmission services should be treated any differently.

Notably, SPP proposes no suspension or disqualification of interruptible loads as part of its

Conditional High Impact Large Loads Service (“CHILLS”).33 If SPP can manage interruptible

loads without such draconian penalties, PJM should similarly be capable of doing so.

            Second, the one reliability incident that PJM highlights to defend its proposal—when

“approximately 1,500 MW of data centers disconnected simultaneously and unexpectedly from

the [Bulk Electric System] due to a transmission line fault in 2024”34—involved traditional grid

co-located with a generator (especially a nuclear generator), it is possible that the load would not

have dropped offline as a result of the load being closer to the voltage source.”36

            Third, PJM fails to explain how its resource adequacy concerns justify its disqualification

and suspension scheme. To the extent PJM’s resource adequacy concerns stem from Interim NITS

and Non-Firm Contract Demand Service being non-capacity backed,37 then PJM should have the

same concern regarding the non-capacity backed loads that could be interconnected under its

Connect and Manage framework and would be required to curtail during capacity shortfalls. But

PJM has proposed no such penalties under the Connect and Manage framework, showing that

PJM’s real agenda here is to discourage use of the transmission services it disfavors.38

            Fourth, a four-month suspension is not “consistent” with NERC requirements as PJM

claims.39 The NERC Reliability Standards that PJM cites—PRC-004-6 (Protection System

Misoperation Identification and Correction) and PRC-012-2 (Remedial Action Schemes)—set

forth a process for investigating whether protection systems misoperated and for developing a

Corrective Action Plan if appropriate.40 Neither Reliability Standard, however, calls for suspension

                     B. Limiting Non-Firm Contract Demand Service to Temporary Derates or
                        Outages Is Non-Compliant and Unreasonable

            PJM claims it must limit Non-Firm Contract Demand Service to temporary derates or

outages because of “the inherent risks to the Transmission System and operational complexities

associated with providing this service on a continuous basis.”41 Based on this logic, PJM should

also limit Non-Firm Point-to-Point Transmission Service. PJM does not. Indeed, if the customer

taking Non-Firm Point-to-Point Transmission Service is willing to pay through congestion, under

the Transmission Loading Relief Procedure, PJM only curtails the service after all other measures

have failed to maintain system reliability.42

Demand Service fares no better. Citing several of PJM’s unsubstantiated claims, Transmission

           Transmission Owners also claim “there is the possibility of interactions between RAS in a

tightly coupled network such as PJM, increasing the possibility of misoperations.”45 This

circumstance is possible but unlikely. Multiple RAS in an area is a sign the transmission

infrastructure is inadequate and the area has increased reliability risks. As Mr. Kormos explained,

“[g]iven the increased reliability risks … most Co-Location Arrangements with new generation

are unlikely to locate in areas without robust transmission.”46

IV.        The Transmission Owners’ Grid Reliance Charge is Based Neither on Principle Nor
           Precedent

           The Commission should reject the Transmission Owners’ Grid Reliance Charge and adopt

the minimum system method as recommended by electricity market expert Zachary Ming.47 The

Transmission Owners’ Grid Reliance Charge is arbitrary and unmoored from cost causation

principles. As Mr. Ming explains in his Reply Testimony in Attachment 1, the Transmission

Owners’ proposal is “an improvised approach lacking any theoretical foundation and disconnected

from any cost-causation principle, designed to produce an outcome that ‘feels right’ to the

Transmission Owners.”48 Their proposal includes all the depreciation costs for the full cost of

            Constellation’s proposal leverages the minimum system method, a principled methodology

grounded in precedent, to produce a just and reasonable rate that ensures Co-Located Loads pay

their fair share of the transmission system based on how they actually use it—which is to receive

ancillary services, not to draw power from the grid. The minimum system method is a “well-

accepted framework for applying cost-causation principles.”52 It is not “extremely challenging to

implement.”53 Numerous jurisdictions across North America have applied the minimum system

method at the distribution level for decades.54 And as Mr. Ming explains, “[t]here is no reason that

it cannot similarly be applied in the context of the transmission system—there has just not

previously been any need to do so.”55

            In his initial testimony, using publicly available data, Mr. Ming estimated that a minimum

system yielding between 2% and 10% of actual system costs is reasonable, and he recommended

a minimum transmission system of 6%.56 The Commission can adopt a Grid Reliance Charge

     V.    Requested Clarifications of PJM’s Response Brief and Modifications to Revised
           Illustrative Tariff

           There are five areas in PJM’s response brief and revised Illustrative Tariff where

clarification is needed or appropriate.

           First, PJM’s statement that an “Interim NITS customer would only be curtailed … if the

system is in an unreliable state due to transmission system violations or capacity/reserve

shortages”57 improperly conflates Interim NITS and the rejected Option 7.58 Under the rejected

Option 7, non-capacity backed loads would have been interconnected on the condition they would

be curtailed before all other load during capacity shortfalls.59 The Commission found this option

“too broad and not sufficiently detailed to direct as a replacement rate.”60 No party, including PJM,

sought rehearing challenging the Commission’s rejection. PJM now attempts to reinstate the

“capacity/reserve shortage” curtailment criterion. But PJM failed to seek rehearing of this issue

and cannot bypass the Federal Power Act’s rehearing requirements.61 The Commission should

reject this attempt62 and direct PJM to revise Part XI, Section 705.2 of its Illustrative Tariff to
